gloss: boy, young man, attendant; girl, maid; youth; shake (off, out); (once) growl
summary: Under one spelling scripture has three groups of words. The great majority are נַעַר and נַעֲרָה: a boy or girl, of any age from a baby in a basket (Exo 2:6) to a young man of fighting age or a girl of marriageable age, and, from that, the young man or young woman who attends a master or mistress, so that Ziba, a father of fifteen sons, is still “the נַעַר of Saul” (2Sa 9:9–10); נְעוּרִים and נֹעַר are youth, the early years of a life or a nation, “the wife of your youth”, Israel's youth in Egypt and the wilderness. The verb נָעַר is to shake: to shake out a fold of a garment, shake off a bribe from the hands, shake oneself free; Yahweh “shook off” the Egyptians in the sea (Exo 14:27), and Jerusalem is told to shake herself from the dust (Isa 52:2); נְעֹרֶת is tow, what is shaken from flax. Once (Jer 51:38) a verb is used of young lions growling. Ugaritic has both nʿr “boy, servant” and nʿr “shake off” with ʿ, and Phoenician nʿr is “young servitor” and nʿrm “youth”; how “boy” and “shake” go together is not understood.

words.gloss: boy, child; young man, youth; attendant, servant; (plural) young men, fighting men
words.summary: About 240 times. The word names a male not yet an elder, whatever his age, from an unborn or newborn child to a young man of seventeen or a king newly crowned; it is set against זָקֵן “old man”. Because the young serve the old, it also names an attendant, a man who serves another, whatever his age. In the Pentateuch the written text also spells the girl נַעַר (read נַעֲרָה; Deu 22:15–29); those tokens are counted under נַעֲרָה.

senses.definition: A male child, from before birth and in infancy through boyhood: a son not yet grown.

evidence.note: Pharaoh's daughter opened the ark “and behold, a נַעַר weeping”: a baby in a basket.
Hannah brought Samuel to Shiloh when he was weaned, “וְהַנַּעַר נָעַר”: the boy was still a child.
Before his birth: “the נַעַר shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb.”
“Teach us what we shall do for the boy who will be born.”
David sought God for the infant son of Bathsheba.
The wife of Phinehas, dying in childbirth, named the boy Ichabod.
“God heard the voice of the boy”: Ishmael, cast out with Hagar, and in 21:20 “God was with the boy, and he grew up.”
“Do not lay your hand on the boy.”
The Shunammite's son: “the boy has not awakened”; in 4:35 “the boy sneezed seven times, and the boy opened his eyes.”
Naaman's flesh “came back like the flesh of a little boy (נַעַר קָטֹן), and he was clean.”
“Before the boy knows to refuse evil and choose good”: the child of Isa 7:14, too young to tell good from evil.
“Before the boy knows to cry ‘My father’ and ‘My mother’.”
“A little boy shall lead them”: the wolf, the lamb, the leopard and the kid together.
Jacob over Ephraim and Manasseh: “the messenger who redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys.”

senses.definition: A male in the years of growing up and of young manhood, set against the old and the experienced: one still under training, not yet of age to lead.

evidence.note: “נַעַר הָיִיתִי גַּם־זָקַנְתִּי, I have been young and now am old.”
“נַעַר וְזָקֵן lie on the ground in the streets.”
“The boy shall be insolent against the elder (בַּזָּקֵן), and the base against the honourable.”
“Joseph, seventeen years old, was shepherding with his brothers … and he was a נַעַר.”
Gideon's firstborn Jether “did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a youth.”
Saul to David: “you are a נַעַר, and he a man of war from his youth (מִנְּעֻרָיו).”
Goliath “despised him, for he was a youth, ruddy and handsome.”
“Whose son are you, הַנַּעַר?”; in 17:56 Saul calls him הָעָלֶם.
Solomon, newly king: “I am a little boy (נַעַר קָטֹן); I do not know how to go out or come in.”
“Solomon my son … is young and tender (נַעַר וָרָךְ), and the work is great.”
“I do not know how to speak, for I am a נַעַר”; Yahweh answers, “Do not say, I am a נַעַר” (1:7).
Josiah, in his eighth year as king, “while he was yet a boy, began to seek the God of David.”
“Woe to you, land, when your king is a boy.”
“I will give boys to be their princes.”
“Youths (נְעָרִים) shall faint and be weary, and chosen young men (בַּחוּרִים) shall stumble”: the strength of youth.
The proverbs were written “to give to the young man knowledge and discretion.”
“Among the sons a young man lacking heart.”
“Train up a boy according to his way; even when he is old (יַזְקִין) he will not depart from it.”
“Folly is bound in the heart of a boy; the rod of discipline will drive it far from him.”
“Even a boy makes himself known by his deeds.”
“How shall a young man make his path clean? By keeping it according to your word.”
“Young men and virgins, old men with boys.”
“The youth shall die a hundred years old.”
“Run, speak to this young man”: the man with the measuring line.
“When Israel was a נַעַר I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son”: the nation in its boyhood.
Hos 11:1 quoted of Jesus, brought back from Egypt: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

senses.definition: A man who attends another and does his bidding: a personal servant, an armour-bearer, a steward, a prophet's or a king's man. The word says what he does for his master, not his age.

evidence.note: “The king called Ziba, Saul's נַעַר”; and 9:10, “Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (עֲבָדִים)”: a נַעַר who was a grown man with a household.
“Ziba, the נַעַר of the house of Saul, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him.”
“Ziba the נַעַר of Mephibosheth.”
“His minister (וּמְשָׁרְתוֹ) Joshua the son of Nun, a נַעַר, did not depart from the tent.”
Abraham “took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son.”
Balaam riding on his donkey, “and his two young men with him.”
Abimelech called “the נַעַר who carried his armour (נֹשֵׂא כֵלָיו)”; also 1Sa 14:1.
“Take with you one of the young men, and arise, go, seek the donkeys.”
“The boy was ministering (מְשָׁרֵת) to Yahweh before Eli the priest.”
“The boy Samuel ministered to Yahweh before Eli.”
“Gehazi, the נַעַר of Elisha the man of God.”
Elisha “said to Gehazi his נַעַר, Call this Shunammite.”
“Boaz said to his נַעַר who was set over the reapers”: the overseer of the harvest.
Solomon saw that the young man Jeroboam was industrious, and set him over all the forced labour of the house of Joseph.
“The king's young men who served him (מְשָׁרְתָיו).”
The former governors burdened the people; “even their young men lorded it over the people.”
“Let every man with his נַעַר lodge within Jerusalem.”
“They struck the young men with the edge of the sword”: Job's servants, also 1:16–17, 19.
“Ask your young men (נְעָרֶיךָ) … let the young men find favour … give to your servants (לַעֲבָדֶיךָ) and to your son David”: נַעַר beside עֶבֶד.
“The words with which the young men of the king of Assyria have reviled me”: the Rabshakeh and his party, called the king's lads (also Isa 37:6).

senses.definition: In the plural, the young men of a leader's company who fight for him.

evidence.note: “By the young men of the governors of the provinces”: they went out first and struck the Arameans (20:15–19).
Abner to Joab: “Let the young men arise and play before us.”
None of the Amalekites escaped “except four hundred young men who rode on camels.”
Abram after the battle of the kings: “except what the young men have eaten.”
David to Ahimelech: “the vessels of the young men are holy.”
David sent ten young men to Nabal.

evidence.locator: Isa.7.16; Isa.8.4; Isa.11.6, הַנַּעַר / נַעַר → παιδίον; Gen.21.12–20; Gen.44.22–34 → παιδίον; παιδίον renders נַעַר ×19

evidence.note: “They saw the child (τὸ παιδίον) with Mary his mother”: Matthew has just quoted Isa 7:14 (Mat 1:23), whose child is הַנַּעַר in Isa 7:16.

evidence.locator: Gen.14.24; Gen.41.12; Num.11.27; Pro.20.11; Lam.5.13, נַעַר → νεανίσκος; νεανίσκος renders נַעַר ×16 in its inflected forms

evidence.note: “I have written to you, young men (νεανίσκοι), because you are strong”: the strength of youth, as Isa 40:30–31.
“The young man says to him, All these I have kept.”
Matthew quotes Hos 11:1 not from this Greek but in the Hebrew's words: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

parallels.note: “Chosen young man”: the young man in his strength, beside נַעַר.
“Young man”: Saul asks of David, whose son is הָעָלֶם, and then asks David, whose son are you, הַנַּעַר.
“Servant”: the attendant beside the servant; Ziba the נַעַר had עֲבָדִים of his own.
“Minister, attendant”: Joshua, Samuel and the king's young men.

opposites.note: “Old man, elder”: young and old, the whole of a people.

phrases.gloss: from young to old: every one

words.gloss: girl, young woman; maid, female attendant
words.summary: About 60 times, the feminine of נַעַר, with the same two sides: a girl or young woman, most often one not yet married or newly married, and the maid who attends a mistress. Like נַעַר it names her age and place, not whether she is a virgin, which is said by adding בְּתוּלָה. No cognate of the feminine has been followed to its own dictionary; it shares the masculine's meaning (kin).

senses.definition: A girl or young woman, from a little girl to a woman of marriageable age; most often one still in her father's house, but also a young wife, a concubine or a young widow.

evidence.note: “The נַעֲרָה was very good of appearance, a virgin (בְּתוּלָה), and no man had known her”: the virginity is added, not contained in the word.
“Let us call the girl and ask her mouth.”
“A little girl (נַעֲרָה קְטַנָּה)” taken captive from Israel, who served Naaman's wife.
Shechem “loved the girl and spoke to the heart of the girl”: Dinah.
In the law of the accused bride: “the father of the girl and her mother.”
He shall give the silver “to the father of the girl, … and she shall be his wife.”
“If there is a נַעֲרָה, a virgin, betrothed to a man”: נַעֲרָה בְתוּלָה, also 22:28.
The Levite's concubine: “the father of the נַעֲרָה saw him.”
“Four hundred young women, virgins, who had not known a man.”
Boaz of Ruth the widow: “Whose is this young woman?”; and 2:6, “she is a young Moabite woman.”
“The seed that Yahweh will give you from this young woman.”
“They found young women going out to draw water.”
“Let them seek for my lord the king a young woman, a virgin”: Abishag (1:3–4).
“Let young women, virgins, good of appearance, be sought for the king.”
Esther: “the young woman was beautiful of form.”
“A man and his father go in to the same girl, to profane my holy name.”

senses.definition: A young woman who attends a mistress or works for a master: a lady's maids, the girls of the harvest field or of a household.

evidence.note: “Rebekah arose, and her young women (וְנַעֲרֹתֶיהָ), and rode on the camels.”
Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe, “and her young women walked beside the river”; she sent her slave-girl (אֲמָתָהּ) for the ark.
Abigail rode on a donkey “with five of her young women who went at her feet.”
Boaz to Ruth: “keep close to my young women”, the girls who gleaned behind his reapers (2:22–23).
“Boaz … with whose young women you were.”
Hegai gave Esther “seven young women” chosen from the king's house.
“I and my young women will fast likewise.”
The woman of valour “gives food to her household and a portion to her young women.”
Wisdom “has sent out her young women; she calls from the heights of the city.”
Of Leviathan: “will you bind him for your young women?”

evidence.locator: Est.2.7, 9, הַנַּעֲרָה → κοράσιον; Est.2.2 נְעָרוֹת → κοράσια

evidence.note: “Talitha koum, which is, Little girl (Τὸ κοράσιον), I say to you, arise”: a girl of twelve (5:42).
“A παιδίσκη named Rhoda came to answer” the door: a maid of the household.

parallels.note: “Virgin”: added to נַעֲרָה where her virginity matters.

words.summary: An abstract plural, about 47 times: the years of being a נַעַר or נַעֲרָה, most often in “from my youth” (the whole of a life so far) and “the wife of your youth”. The prophets use it of Israel's beginnings in Egypt and the wilderness. Jer 32:30 has the feminine plural נְעֻרֹת in the same sense; BDB lists that form separately (n.ei.af) but its key counts the same tokens, so it is not named here.

senses.gloss: youth, the early years of a life
senses.definition: The time when one is young; with מִן, the whole of a life from its beginning to now.

evidence.note: “You are a נַעַר, and he a man of war מִנְּעֻרָיו.”
“Your servants have been men of livestock from our youth until now.”
Samuel: “I have walked before you from my youth until this day.”
Obadiah: “your servant has feared Yahweh from my youth.”
“You are my hope, Lord Yahweh, my trust from my youth”; 71:17, “you have taught me from my youth.”
“It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.”
“Your youth is renewed like the eagle's.”
“As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of youth.”
A priest's daughter widowed or divorced, with no child, returns “to her father's house as in her youth.”
A woman's vow “in her father's house, in her youth.”
“A man acquired me from my youth.”
“Many times they have afflicted me from my youth, let Israel now say.”

senses.gloss: youth as the time of first sins
senses.definition: The beginning of a life as the time its sins begin: what a man did in his youth is remembered against him, or he asks that it not be.

evidence.note: “The inclination (יֵצֶר) of the heart of man is evil from his youth.”
“Do not remember the sins of my youth and my transgressions.”
“You make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.”
“We have sinned against Yahweh our God, we and our fathers, from our youth until this day.”
Ephraim: “I bore the reproach of my youth.”
“This has been your way from your youth, that you did not listen to my voice.”
“The sons of Israel and the sons of Judah have done only evil in my eyes from their youth (מִנְּעֻרֹתֵיהֶם)”: the feminine plural.

senses.definition: The one married in youth, to whom the covenant of marriage binds for life.

evidence.note: “Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.”
“Rejoice with the wife of your youth.”
The strange woman “forsakes the companion (אַלּוּף) of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God.”
“Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.”
“Like a wife of youth when she is rejected, says your God.”

senses.gloss: the youth of Israel (Egypt and the wilderness)
senses.definition: The nation's beginnings: its time in Egypt, the exodus and the wilderness, remembered as the youth of a bride or as a youth of harlotry.

evidence.note: “I remember the kindness of your youth, the love of your betrothals, your going after me in the wilderness.”
“She shall answer there as in the days of her youth, as in the day she came up from the land of Egypt.”
“You did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and bare.”
“I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you.”
“They played the harlot in Egypt; in their youth they played the harlot.”
“My father, you are the companion of my youth.”
Of Moab: “at ease from his youth … he has not gone into exile.”
Of Babylon: “your sorceries, with which you have laboured from your youth.”

evidence.locator: 1Sa.12.2; 1Sa.17.33; 1Ki.18.12; Psa.71.5, 17; Job.31.18, נְעוּרִים → νεότης; νεότης renders נְעוּרִים ×29

evidence.note: “All these I have kept from my youth (ἐκ νεότητός μου)”: the Hebrew's מִנְּעוּרַי.
“My manner of life from my youth … all the Jews know.”
“Let no one despise your youth”: as Yahweh to Jeremiah, “do not say, I am a נַעַר” (Jer 1:7).

phrases.gloss: from my youth: all my life

words.summary: Four times, in poetry: the same as נְעוּרִים.

senses.definition: The young years of a life; with מִן, from youth on.

evidence.note: “His flesh becomes fresher than a child's (מִנֹּעַר); he returns to the days of his youth (עֲלוּמָיו).”
“I am afflicted and ready to die from youth.”
“He who pampers his servant from youth (מִנֹּעַר), at his end he will be מָנוֹן”: a word not otherwise known.
The godless: “their soul (נַפְשָׁם) dies in youth, and their life among the cult prostitutes.”

words.gloss: shake, shake out, shake off; (niphal, hithpael) shake oneself (free)
words.summary: Eleven times. To shake something so that what is in it or on it falls out or off: a fold of a garment emptied, a bribe shaken off the hands, the leaves of a forest, the wicked out of the earth, Egypt into the sea; reflexive, to shake oneself free. The link with נַעַר “boy” is not yet understood: Ugaritic has both, with the same ʿ.

senses.definition: To shake a thing so that what it holds falls out, or what clings to it falls off.

evidence.note: “I shook out (נָעַרְתִּי) my lap and said, So may God shake out (יְנַעֵר) every man from his house and his labour who does not keep this word; even so may he be shaken out (נָעוּר) and empty (וָרֵק).”
The righteous man “shakes his palms (נֹעֵר כַּפָּיו) from holding a bribe.”
“Lebanon is ashamed and withers; Sharon is like the Arabah, and Bashan and Carmel shake off (their leaves).”

stems.gloss: be shaken off, shaken out; shake oneself (free)

senses.gloss: be shaken off; shake oneself free
senses.definition: To be shaken off or out like something worthless; or, reflexive, to shake oneself free of what binds.

evidence.note: Samson woke: “I will go out as at other times and shake myself free (וְאִנָּעֵר)”, not knowing that Yahweh had turned from him.
“Like a shadow when it lengthens I am gone; I am shaken off like a locust.”
The dawn takes hold of the edges of the earth “and the wicked are shaken out of it”, like dust from a cloth.

senses.definition: Of God: to shake men off or out as a man shakes out a cloth, in judgment.

evidence.note: “The Egyptians fled toward it, וַיְנַעֵר יַהְוֶה אֶת־מִצְרַיִם in the midst of the sea.”
“וְנִעֵר Pharaoh and his army in the Sea of Reeds, for his kindness is for ever.”
“So may God shake out every man from his house.”

senses.definition: To shake oneself, so that what lies on one falls away.

evidence.note: “הִתְנַעֲרִי מֵעָפָר, arise, sit, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion.”

evidence.locator: Exo.14.27; Jdg.16.20; Neh.5.13 (three times); Job.38.13; Psa.109.23; Psa.136.15; Isa.52.2, נָעַר → ἐκτινάσσω

evidence.note: When the Jews of Corinth opposed him, Paul “shook out his garments (ἐκτιναξάμενος τὰ ἱμάτια)”: Nehemiah's act of Neh 5:13.
“They shook off the dust of their feet against them.”
“Shake off the dust of your feet.”

parallels.note: “Empty”: what is shaken out is left empty.
“Loose”: shake off the dust, loose the bonds.

words.summary: Twice. The coarse fibre of flax, which snaps or burns at the touch of fire; read as what is shaken off the flax when it is beaten, so kin to the verb.

senses.definition: Flax fibre, weak and quick to burn.

evidence.note: Samson snapped the bowstrings “as a thread of tow (פְּתִיל־הַנְּעֹרֶת) snaps when it smells fire.”
“The strong man shall become tow, and his work a spark, and both shall burn together, and none shall quench them.”

words.gloss: the scattered (?); or the young (of the flock)
words.summary: Once (Zec 11:16), if it is a separate word. Among the sheep the foolish shepherd will neglect, “the perishing he will not visit, הַנַּעַר he will not seek, the broken he will not heal”, it stands where Ezk 34:4, 16 has “the driven away” and “the lost”: so read as what is shaken out, scattered. It may as well be נַעַר “young” of the young of the flock. BDB's key n.eh.ab is not named, because it counts every token spelled like נַעַר “boy”.

senses.definition: In the list of the sheep a shepherd should care for: one that is to be sought.

evidence.note: “The perishing he will not visit, הַנַּעַר he will not seek, the broken he will not heal, the standing he will not sustain.”
“The driven away (הַנִּדַּחַת) you have not brought back, and the lost you have not sought.”

words.summary: Once, of lions' cubs, beside שָׁאַג “roar”. Arabic naʿara “make a sound in the nose, cry out” and Akkadian naʾāru “roar” share the meaning; it may be a root of its own in the same spelling. Its link to “boy” and “shake” is not known.

senses.definition: Of young lions: to growl, a sound beside a roar.

evidence.note: Of the Babylonians: “together they shall roar (יִשְׁאֲגוּ) like young lions, they shall growl (נָעֲרוּ) like lions' whelps.”

cognates.note: /naʿr-/, in letters and administrative texts (KTU 2.33:20; 4.360:5); Segert sets it beside Hebrew נַעַר and Phoenician nʿr. The same two sides as the Hebrew, boy and servant. Ugaritic writes ʿ and ġ with different signs.
The D stem, as the Hebrew piel, in KTU 1.100:65. The same ʿ as nʿr “boy”: Ugaritic gives no sign that the two are separate older roots.

evidence.note: “D ynʿrnh 1.100:65 = 86.73 ‘to shake off’ (H. n-ʿ-r Pi.).”

cognates.note: Phoenician, on the Kition temple tariff, “to the three young servitors, three qp” (KAI 37 A 12); Neo-Punic “his son” (IRT 889). The attendant of the Hebrew, and the boy.

evidence.note: “[Heb. naʿar] n.m. 1. YOUNG SERVITOR in a temple … 2. SON.”

cognates.note: Kilamuwa of Samal: “he who had never owned a tunic from his youth (lmnʿry), in my days was clothed in byssus” (KAI 24.12–13): the Hebrew's “from my youth”, with the same plural.

evidence.note: “[Heb. neʿurim] n.pl. YOUTH.”

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic of the Talmud and Midrash: “let him shake the fruit out of the basket” (Sabb. 142a). The Hebrew's shaking out until empty (Neh 5:13). Aramaic writes ʿ for both older sounds.

evidence.locator: s.v. נְעַר (ch.), citing Targ. Job XXI, 32; Sabb. 142a (Pa. וְלִינַעֲרִינְהוּ נַעוּרֵי)
evidence.note: “to shake, stir … Pa. to shake; to empty.”

cognates.gloss: utter a sound in the inner nose; cry out vehemently; (a vein) gush with a noise; (naʿra) a sound in the nose
cognates.note: A sound from the throat or nose, of a man or a beast: the growl of Jer 51:38. Lane's other uses (a vein gushing with blood; nāʿūr, a creaking water-wheel) are of noise too. Arabic shows ʿ, not ġ. Arabic نَغَرَ “boil, be agitated” (with ġ) is not taken as a cognate of the shaking verb, which Ugaritic writes with ʿ.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2815, art. نعر, نَعَرَ (n40098)
evidence.note: “He (a man, or a beast of carriage) uttered a sound, or noise, with, or in, his خَيْشُوم [or the innermost part of his nose] … He called out, or cried out vehemently, in war, or in some evil case.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2815, art. نعر, نَعْرَةٌ (n40099)
evidence.note: “A sound, or noise, in the خَيْشُوم.”

evidence.locator: Arabic نعر (naʕara), verb: to emit a sound through the nose, to snort, to grunt; to roar, to howl, to hoot, to bellow

cognates.note: Middle and Neo-Assyrian. Akkadian writes ʾ where the other languages have ʿ, so it cannot show which older sound stands behind ע.

evidence.note: Meanings in the glossaries: roar, roaring; written forms naʾārum, unaʾʾurū, uttaʾʾar, uttâr.

doctrine.statement: Isaiah 65 describes what Yahweh will create: “I create Jerusalem a rejoicing and her people a joy … the voice of weeping shall no more be heard in her” (Isa 65:18–19). In that Jerusalem “there shall be no more an infant of days, nor an old man who has not filled his days, for the youth (הַנַּעַר) shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa 65:20); men build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, bear children, and “the wolf and the lamb shall feed together” (Isa 65:21–25). Isaiah 11 says the same of the reign of the shoot from the stump of Jesse: “a little boy (נַעַר קָטֹן) shall lead them … for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of Yahweh as the waters cover the sea” (Isa 11:1, 6–9). From the verses: the kingdom is on the earth, centred in Jerusalem, under the Son of David; in it there are still mortal people who are born, grow from boyhood, live very long, and die, and sin is still judged.

“When Israel was a נַעַר I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos 11:1): Yahweh's son Israel (Exo 4:22) had a boyhood, its time in Egypt and the wilderness, the “days of her youth” (Jer 2:2; Hos 2:17). Matthew says Jesus' return from Egypt “fulfilled what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, Out of Egypt I called my son” (Mat 2:15): the Son of God lived Israel's history from its beginning. He too was a boy. Of the boy Samuel scripture says, “the boy (וְהַנַּעַר) Samuel grew on and was in favour both with Yahweh and with men” (1Sa 2:26), and Luke says the same of Jesus: “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men” (Luk 2:52; also 2:40). From the verses: the Son of God was born, was a child, and grew in wisdom as a boy grows; his sonship is traced, as Israel's was, from his birth and his calling out of Egypt, not from an existence before it.

After the flood Yahweh said, “the inclination (יֵצֶר) of the heart of man is evil from his youth (מִנְּעֻרָיו)” (Gen 8:21). The sinner's prayer is “do not remember the sins of my youth” (Psa 25:7); Job speaks of “the iniquities of my youth” (Job 13:26); Israel confesses, “we have sinned … from our youth until this day” (Jer 3:25). “Folly is bound in the heart of a boy; the rod of discipline will drive it far from him” (Pro 22:15), and “how shall a young man make his path clean? By keeping it according to your word” (Psa 119:9). From the verses: the bent toward sin is in man's own heart from the beginning of his life, and is not brought to him from outside; what answers it is discipline and the word of God.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key נער, the brief's key. BDB keys: n.ei.ab (נַעַר) is named; n.eh.ab (נַעַר “shaking, scattered ones”) counts 63 tokens that are נַעַר “boy” by spelling, while BDB itself gives it only Zec 11:16, so the word is kept without its key. n.ei.af (נְעוּרוֹת) lists the same 47 tokens as n.ei.ae; n.ei.ae is named, and Jer 32:30 is cited under נְעוּרִים. The Pentateuch's written נַעַר for the girl (read נַעֲרָה, Deu 22) is counted by the database under n.ei.ad. Names: names/naarah.json (n.ei.ah, left off it because it counts the 14 tokens spelled נַעֲרָה, the girl, as well), names/neariah.json (n.ei.aj), names/naarai.json (n.ei.ai). Places left out: נַעֲרָה Naarah (n.ei.ag, Jos 16:7; its key also counts the girl) and נַעֲרָן Naaran (n.ei.ak, 1Ch 7:28), probably the same town (TIPNR Naaran@Jos.16.7). Left out: נֶפֶג Nepheg (n.ei.am), filed here only by alphabetical position; its root is נפג. Open questions: (1) whether נַעַר “boy” and נָעַר “shake” are one root. Ugaritic has both with ʿ (Segert p. 194), so the cognates do not split them; a link (the boy as one “stirred up”, or the shaken-off?) has no evidence. (2) Whether נָעַר “growl” (Jer 51:38) is a separate root; Arabic naʿara and Akkadian naʾāru support the sound sense, but the Arabic ʿ is the same as the others. (3) Zec 11:16: “the scattered” or “the young”. Leads not followed: Ugaritic nʿrt “maidservant” (Wiktionary's link from Hebrew נַעֲרָה, not in Segert's glossary; DULAT not consulted); Egyptian n-ꜥ-r-n (Semitic loan for “young soldiers” in New Kingdom texts) not looked up in TLA; Lane's نَاعُور “water-wheel”, which Wiktionary derives from Syriac, not followed; Syriac has no nʿr in SEDRA. Jewish Aramaic נְעַר and the post-biblical Hebrew נָעַר “bray” (Jastrow) are leads for the growl verb but the latter is Hebrew, not a cognate.
